claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu coatings transition from stable to unstable wear through a shift from defect-mediated plasticity to rapid lattice disorder.
The mechanism shift occurs at a critical temperature of approximately 400–500 K.
Below the critical temperature, high stacking-fault energy stabilizes dislocation structures.
Below the critical temperature, sluggish diffusion helps stabilize dislocation structures.
Stabilized dislocation structures maintain high elastic modulus and wear resistance.
Increasing temperature reduces the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu.
The reduction in stacking-fault energy promotes dislocation cross-slip and annihilation.
Lattice softening and enhanced atomic diffusion produce rapid atomic disorder.
Rapid atomic disorder causes loss of structural integrity and catastrophic wear failure.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is an FCC single-phase material.
The initial coating has a high dislocation density produced by deposition.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating is stable at 300 K.
Low-temperature dislocation glide and stacking-fault formation enable work hardening and wear resistance.
Wear resistance declines sharply above approximately 450 K.
Conventional high-entropy alloys generally show gradual degradation with increasing temperature.
FeNiCrCoCu has a sharper temperature-driven wear transition than conventional HEAs because of unique stacking-fault-energy behavior.
The proposed mechanism is limited to FeNiCrCoCu coatings on Cu matrices under sliding wear and may not apply to refractory HEAs or other matrices.
The critical temperature may vary with coating microstructure, Cu-matrix interactions, and alloy composition ratios.
Direct experimental data for FeNiCrCoCu under combined elevated-temperature nanoindentation and friction are limited.
A gradual rather than sharp wear decline, or stable dislocation density with increasing temperature, would falsify the hypothesis.
